lessons.name: How does matter move in food chains?

contents.text: A food chain is a model. A model can be used to represent events in nature and make these events easier to understand. A food chain is a model that shows where organisms in an ecosystem get their food.
A food chain has arrows that point from one organism to another. Each arrow shows the direction that matter moves when one organism eats another organism.

Matter enters a food chain when a producer makes its own food. This is how all of the matter eaten by organisms enters the food chain. Many producers make their own food using carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight. Producers do not eat other organisms, so there is no arrow pointing from another organism to the producer in a food chain.
Matter first moves up a food chain when the producer is eaten by a consumer. This is shown by an arrow pointing from the producer to a consumer.

header.text: Matter moves further up a food chain when a consumer eats another consumer. This is shown by an arrow pointing from one consumer to another consumer in the food chain. A food chain can have several kinds of consumers. Each kind of consumer can be described by what it eats:

contents.text: A primary consumer eats the producer. So, there is an arrow pointing from the producer to the primary consumer in a food chain.
A secondary consumer eats the primary consumer. So, there is an arrow pointing from the primary consumer to the secondary consumer in a food chain.
A tertiary consumer eats the secondary consumer. So, there is an arrow pointing from the secondary consumer to the tertiary consumer in a food chain.
A top consumer is the animal at the top of a food chain. So, there is no arrow pointing to an organism that eats the top consumer.
A consumer that hunts and eats another consumer is a predator. The consumer eaten by a predator is its prey. Matter moves up a food chain when a predator hunts and eats its prey.

shows where organisms in an ecosystem get their food. Models can make things in nature easier to understand because models can represent complex things in a simpler way. If a food web showed every organism in an ecosystem, the food web would be hard to understand. So, each food web shows how some organisms in an ecosystem can get their food.

When one organism eats another, energy moves from the consumed organism's body to the
body. After this, the energy often gets
, or converted into other types of energy. For example, when a kelp bass eats kelp, chemical energy from the kelp's body tissues can be transformed into mechanical energy within the bass's body.
Energy that organisms consume and then store in their body tissues as chemical energy has been
to their trophic level. But only about

of the energy present in the body tissues of organisms in one trophic level gets transferred to the next trophic level. Since energy is always conserved, how can there be varying amounts of energy present in different trophic levels?
About

of the chemical energy consumers obtain from eating food is ultimately released to the environment as waste or heat. For example, when a sea otter eats a sea urchin, the otter may only break down about
of the chemical energy stored in the urchin's body. The other half of the chemical energy is in indigestible tissues that pass through the otter's digestive system as waste.

Most of the chemical energy that the otter breaks down is used for cellular respiration and other functions, such as digestion and movement, which release heat as a byproduct. The little energy that remains, about
of what was originally consumed, is stored in the otter's body tissues as it grows. This energy is available to be transferred to the next trophic level when the otter is eaten.

To get the nutrients it needs to survive, the plant uses a pitcher-shaped leaf as a trap to catch and digest small organisms. But the plant can also get nutrients from other sources, including from the feces of woolly bats.

, or settle to sleep, in the upper part of the plant's trap. In the trap, the bat is protected from predators and bad weather. The plant then absorbs nutrients from the digested feces.

textContent.text: A rat tapeworm is a type of flatworm that can live inside a rat's body. When a rat eats an insect that has a tapeworm inside it, the insect is digested, but the tapeworm remains alive.

The tapeworm is moved into the rat's intestines and uses suckers to attach itself to the intestine wall. Inside the rat's intestine, the tapeworm absorbs nutrients from food that the rat has eaten. If the rat has many tapeworms in its intestines, it will become weak from lack of nutrients.

textContent.text: White sea urchins live in tropical oceans. Sea urchins are covered with hard, sharp spines. These spear-like spines protect the sea urchin from predators, such as fish. Sometimes a small worm, called a bristle worm, also uses the spines for protection.

The worm lives on the sea urchin, between the spines. To attack a worm on the sea urchin's body, a fish would have to get past the spines. When the worm lives on the sea urchin, the worm does not change the sea urchin's ability to survive.

textContent.text: Cleaner wrasse are small fish that live in tropical coral reefs. Wrasse are often visited by larger fish, such as moray eels.
When an eel visits a wrasse, the wrasse cleans the eel by eating parasites attached to the eel's body. If the parasites are not removed, the eel may become weak or even die.

Before the wrasse begins to clean, the eel opens its mouth to signal to the wrasse that it is ready to be cleaned. Then the wrasse eats all the parasites it can find on the eel's body, including those inside the eel's mouth!

lessons.name: Investigate primary succession on a volcanic island

pieces.text: Before sunrise on November 14, 1963, the crew of the fishing boat

had just finished putting their fishing lines in the ocean off the southern coast of Iceland. As the crew waited to have breakfast, a strong smell of sulfur drifted over the boat. At first, crew members thought that the cook had burned the eggs or that something was wrong with the boat's engine. But when the sun started to rise, the crew saw black smoke billowing from the water a few kilometers away.
The captain of the
first thought the smoke was coming from a boat that was on fire, so he sailed closer to try to help. But as the

approached the column of smoke, the captain and crew saw glowing pieces of molten rock shooting up out of the water. The captain realized this was not a burning boat. It was a volcano erupting under the water!

Erupting volcanoes often release molten rock and gases that smell strongly of sulfur. So, when the captain noticed these things, he was observing evidence of a volcanic eruption.

contents.text: The volcano continued to erupt. By November 20, 1963—just six days after the volcano first erupted—it had produced enough lava and ash to form an island that rose 70 meters above the ocean's surface. The volcano finally stopped erupting in 1967.

This newly formed island, called Surtsey, is located 33 kilometers off the southern coast of Iceland. Surtsey has a cold, harsh environment. In the winter, the temperature is often just above freezing, and in the summer, it rarely gets above 50℉. Surtsey is also a very windy place. High winds near the island help create large waves that scour the coastline.

contents.text: The process of primary succession begins when organisms first start to live in an environment that was sterile. Primary succession continues as the number and type of organisms living in the environment change over time.

contents.text: When Surtsey first formed, there were no organisms living on the island. Other than microorganisms, the first organisms to live on the island were plants, which arrived when they were still seeds. Seeds got to Surtsey in different ways, including by drifting on currents in the ocean. Ocean currents likely carried the first seeds that grew and survived long enough to reproduce on Surtsey.

pieces.text: Seeds from many species of plants drifted on ocean currents from Iceland to Surtsey. But only some of these plants were able to
, or move onto and reproduce on, the new island. These species of plants are examples of pioneer species. A
is an organism that can colonize either a new environment or an environment where the ecosystem was destroyed.

contents.text: Pioneer species have traits that allow them to survive in environments that are too harsh for most species. The traits that allow a pioneer species to colonize a new environment depend on the conditions of that environment.

To have been a pioneer species on Surtsey, seeds needed to germinate and grow in rocky soil with few nutrients. Most of the seeds that arrived on Surtsey did not have traits that allowed them to be pioneer species there.

explanationText.text: Many of the nutrients found in soil come from rocks that have eroded over time and from the bodies of organisms that have decomposed. So, the ability to germinate in rocky soil with few nutrients would help a seed successfully colonize the island.

first thought the smoke was coming from a boat that was on fire, so he sailed closer to try to help. But as the

approached the column of smoke, the captain and crew saw glowing pieces of molten rock shooting up out of the water. The captain realized this was not a burning boat. It was a volcano erupting under the water!

contents.text: The volcano continued to erupt. By November 20, 1963—just six days after the volcano first erupted—it had produced enough lava and ash to form an island that rose 70 meters above the ocean's surface. The volcano finally stopped erupting in 1967.

This newly formed island, called Surtsey, is located 33 kilometers off the southern coast of Iceland. Surtsey has a cold, harsh environment. In the winter, the temperature is often just above freezing, and in the summer, it rarely gets above 50℉. Surtsey is also a very windy place. High winds near the island help create large waves that scour the coastline.

This newly formed island, called Surtsey, is located 33 kilometers off the southern coast of Iceland. Surtsey has a cold, harsh environment. In the winter, the temperature is often just above freezing, and in the summer, it rarely gets above 50℉. Surtsey is also a very windy place. High winds near the island help create large waves that scour the coastline.

pieces.text: Seeds from many species of plants drifted on ocean currents from Iceland to Surtsey. But only some of these plants were able to
, or move onto and reproduce on, the new island. These species of plants are examples of pioneer species. A
is an organism that can colonize either a new environment or an environment where the ecosystem was destroyed.

contents.text: Pioneer species have traits that allow them to survive in environments that are too harsh for most species. The traits that allow a pioneer species to colonize a new environment depend on the conditions of that environment.

To have been a pioneer species on Surtsey, seeds needed to germinate and grow in rocky soil with few nutrients. Most of the seeds that arrived on Surtsey did not have traits that allowed them to be pioneer species there.

contents.text: Look at the photographs to help you fill in the table.

The photograph of Surtsey in 2014 shows an ecosystem that contained many organisms, including plants. Over many years, an ecosystem began to form on Surtsey. This ecosystem contained plants, insects, and birds.
The photograph of Surtsey in 1963 shows a sterile environment covered in lava, hot rocks, and ash.
